section.title: David's Victories
section.sectionRationale: Fresh from the everlasting covenant of chapter 17, the Chronicler shows what that covenant looks like on the ground: David subdues the nations pressing in on every side, Philistia, Moab, Zobah, Aram, Hamath, Edom, and gathers gold and silver that he dedicates to the LORD rather than to himself. The chapter closes with a roll call of David's officials who administer justice and righteousness for the whole nation. For the exiles reading Chronicles centuries later, this is not mere military history; it is proof that the covenant God who promised David rest and a name kept His word.
section.thesis: Twice the Chronicler states the refrain that explains everything: the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. David's empire, his dedicated plunder, and his just administration are not achievements to David's own credit but visible evidence of God's covenant faithfulness, an idealized portrait of the king who prefigures the greater Son of David whose victory and righteous reign will have no end.
section.frameNote: Four beats: victory over Philistia and Moab, verses 1 to 2; the defeat of Zobah, Damascus, and Hamath's tribute, verses 3 to 11; victory over Edom, verses 12 to 13; and the roster of David's officials who administer justice and righteousness, verses 14 to 17.

verses.text: Some time later, David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Gath and its villages from the hand of the Philistines.
David also defeated the Moabites, and they became subject to David and brought him {{mas|tribute}}.

units.label: Zobah, Damascus, and Hamath
units.note: the LORD made David victorious wherever he went

verses.text: As far as Hamath, David also defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah, who had marched out to establish his dominion along the Euphrates River.
David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men.
Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David {{yasha|victorious}} wherever he went.
And David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.
And from Tibhath and Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles.
When King Tou of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer king of Zobah,
he sent his son Hadoram to greet King David and bless him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Tou. Hadoram brought all kinds of articles of gold and silver and bronze,

and King David {{qadash|dedicated}} these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had carried off from all these nations, from Edom and Moab, and from the Ammonites, Philistines, and Amalekites.
Moreover, Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He placed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.

units.label: David's officials
units.note: justice and righteousness for all his people

verses.text: Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people:
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder;
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was the scribe;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David's sons were chief officials at the king's side.

yasha.gloss: To save, deliver, or give victory. The BSB footnote notes the phrase can equally be rendered 'the LORD saved David wherever he went.' The Chronicler wants readers to see past David's own generalship: it is the LORD who saves and gives victory, the same root that later gives us the name Yeshua, Jesus, the LORD saves.

qadash.gloss: To consecrate, dedicate, or set apart as holy. David dedicates the plundered gold and silver to the LORD rather than keeping it for himself, foreshadowing the very metals Solomon will use to build the temple, 1 Chronicles 18:8.

mas.gloss: Forced labor or tribute paid by a subject people. Moab, Aram, and Edom all become subject to David and bring him tribute, a visible sign of the dominion and rest God is giving David's throne, in keeping with the covenant of chapter 17.

basic.context: This chapter follows immediately after God's covenant promise to David in chapter 17, that He would give David rest from his enemies and build him an everlasting house. Chapter 18 shows that promise beginning to be kept in real history: David defeats the Philistines, Moab, the Arameans of Zobah and Damascus, and Edom, and the surrounding kings either pay him tribute or send gifts of homage. Twice the text says plainly, 'the LORD made David victorious wherever he went,' so that no reader mistakes these wins for David's own cleverness or strength. Rather than keeping the plunder, David dedicates the gold and silver to the LORD, some of which Solomon will later use to build the temple. The chapter closes with a list of David's chief officials, summarized by the note that David 'administered justice and righteousness for all his people.' Key questions the passage raises: why does the Chronicler repeat 'the LORD made David victorious'? What does it mean that the plunder is dedicated to the LORD rather than spent? And why end a war chapter with a list of civil officials?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, closely paralleling 2 Samuel 8, but the Chronicler, writing generations later for the returned exiles, retells it to highlight God's faithfulness rather than to add new information. The refrain 'the LORD made David victorious' is the Chronicler's own theological commentary built into the narration. The chapter describes what happened; it is not prescribing warfare as a spiritual pattern for believers, but it does teach the enduring truth that all victory, security, and just government come from God's hand, not human strength.
basic.originalLanguages: The key phrase 'the LORD made David victorious,' hoshia, comes from the same root, yasha, that gives Jesus His name, the LORD saves. David's gathered gold he 'dedicated,' qadash, set apart as holy, to the LORD rather than to himself. And the nations that submit bring mas, tribute, a visible sign of David's God given dominion.
basic.typology: David's victories over every surrounding enemy, achieved not by his own strength but by the LORD who saves, prefigure the greater Son of David who triumphs fully and finally over every hostile power, Colossians 2:15. The gold and bronze David dedicates for the future temple anticipate Christ, who is Himself building a greater house, His church, out of the spoils of His victory.
basic.christ: The refrain 'the LORD made David victorious wherever he went' points to a king whose success is entirely of grace, a pattern completed in Jesus, the Son of David, whose victory over sin, death, and every hostile power is total, Colossians 2:15, and whose kingdom of justice and righteousness will never end, Isaiah 9:7. David dedicating his plunder to the LORD, rather than spending it on himself, pictures the self giving generosity fulfilled in Christ, who pours out everything He has for His people.
basic.god: God is the true source of every victory; David's repeated wins are credited not to superior armies but to the LORD who saves. God is also the God of justice, seen in David's just administration, and the God who receives what is dedicated to Him, turning war plunder into temple materials for His future house.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 8 gives the parallel account of these same wars. Psalm 60's superscription is set during this very conflict with Aram and Edom, showing David turning to prayer even amid these victories. Colossians 2:15 says Christ triumphed over the rulers and authorities. Isaiah 9:7 promises a Son of David whose government of justice and righteousness will never end.
basic.oneStory: David's victories are proof, in real history, that the covenant God made with him in chapter 17 was already being kept: rest from every enemy and a name among the great. That covenant faithfulness reaches its fullest expression in Jesus, the Son of David, whose victory over every enemy is total and whose righteous reign will never end.

context.literary:
Chapter 18 opens a run of war narratives, chapters 18 to 20, sandwiched between the covenant of chapter 17 and the tragic census of chapter 21. Structurally it moves outward in a circuit, Philistia to the west, Moab to the east, Zobah and Damascus to the north, Edom to the south, before closing with a list of officials that answers the opening formula 'administered justice and righteousness for all his people.'

The unit is framed by two refrains, "the LORD made David victorious wherever he went," verses 6 and 13, which divide the chapter's four campaigns into two matching panels, each ending on that same verdict, so that even readers skimming the list of names and numbers cannot miss whose victory it actually was. Between the refrains the geography moves outward from every point of the compass, Philistia west, Moab east, Zobah and Damascus north, Edom south, an encircling sweep that leaves David's kingdom, by the chapter's end, secure on every side, precisely the rest from all his enemies promised in the chapter just before. The closing list of officials, verses 14 to 17, answers the chapter's opening formula, "David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness," so that the movement of the whole unit runs from war to peace, from conquest to competent, ordered government, refusing to let military success stand as the chapter's last word.
context.historical:
These campaigns correspond closely to 2 Samuel 8, fought in the tenth century BC as David consolidated a regional empire stretching from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. The plunder David dedicates, especially the bronze from Tibhath and Cun, directly supplies materials Solomon later used for the temple's bronze Sea and pillars, 1 Chronicles 18:8, tying this military chapter directly to the building project the exiles cared about most.

The kingdoms David subdues here were not minor local chiefdoms. Zobah, under Hadadezer, was pressing to extend its own dominion to the Euphrates when David met it, verse 3, meaning David's victory checked a rival empire at the very moment it was expanding, not merely a border skirmish. The scale of the captured force, a thousand chariots and twenty thousand foot soldiers, verse 4, indicates a serious regional power, and David's decision to hamstring all but a hundred of the chariot horses, rather than build his own massive chariot corps, marks a deliberate restraint, keeping Israel's military dependent on the LORD's help rather than on imported cavalry technology, the very temptation later kings, and the Torah itself, warn against, Deuteronomy 17:16. Tou of Hamath's voluntary gift embassy, sending his own son to bless David, verses 9 to 10, reflects the normal diplomatic practice by which smaller kingdoms secured goodwill with a rising regional power without direct conquest, evidence that David's reputation was doing work his armies did not have to.
context.canonical:
The Chronicler omits nearly everything from 2 Samuel 9 to 20, the family and court troubles that follow David's sin, and moves straight from covenant to conquest to temple preparation. This is part of the Chronicler's idealized portrait of David as the righteous, victorious king whose reign anticipates the perfect and final Son of David, Jesus the Messiah.

This chapter also quietly supplies Solomon's building materials before Solomon is even introduced as a candidate for the throne. The bronze from Tibhath and Cun, verse 8, resurfaces explicitly a generation later, used for the bronze Sea, the pillars, and the temple's bronze articles, 2 Chronicles 4:11-18, so that the Chronicler is already, in a war chapter, preparing his readers for the temple narrative still ten chapters away. The same pattern recurs with the officials list; Zadok, first named here alongside Ahimelech, becomes part of the priestly line the Chronicler traces with special care through the rest of the book, and Benaiah, commanding David's foreign guard here, later secures Solomon's own succession, 1 Kings 1:32-40. Nothing in this chapter is a loose end; every name and every dedicated ingot points forward into the story the Chronicler is still telling.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To demonstrate, through a rapid summary of real victories and a properly ordered administration, that God was faithfully keeping His covenant promise of rest and a great name for David, given just one chapter earlier, and to present David as the ideal king whose success flows entirely from the LORD.

The Chronicler also wants his exilic readers to see that God's gifts of victory and dominion were never meant to terminate on David's own glory. Twice interrupting his own narrative to credit the LORD rather than David is a rhetorical choice, not a neutral report; a purely military historian would have named strategy, numbers, or terrain. By naming God as the acting subject of David's verbs, the Chronicler teaches a community with no army and no empire of its own that the same God who once gave dominion to David had not changed in nature, only in the shape of what He was presently giving, so that security for the return community would have to be sought the same way David's had been secured, in trust rather than in strength they did not possess.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes ancient Near Eastern warfare and tribute systems; it does not prescribe a pattern of conquest for believers today. What endures is the theology behind the history: that God alone gives victory, that plunder rightly belongs to Him, and that just government is a gift from His hand.

Nor does the chapter prescribe dedicating literal war spoils to religious building projects as a timeless pattern; David's action was fitting to his moment and his coming son's specific calling to build the temple, not a general rule that all gain must be funneled into construction. What does carry forward as abiding instruction is the underlying posture the action expresses: refusing to let victory, income, or increase become simply personal property, and instead treating it as something held in trust, available to be set apart for God's purposes, whatever concrete shape that takes in a reader's own circumstances, since the New Testament transposes exactly this instinct into ordinary generosity and stewardship, 2 Corinthians 9:6-8.

debates.question: Why does the Chronicler place this whole military survey immediately after the Davidic covenant of chapter 17?

views.label: Immediate proof of covenant fulfillment
views.case: God had just promised David rest from his enemies and a great name, 17:8-10; chapter 18 shows that promise already being kept in tangible history, so the exiles reading Chronicles see that God's covenant word does not return empty.

views.label: Following the Chronicler's inherited source order
views.case: The material closely tracks 2 Samuel 8, so some see the sequence as simply following the Chronicler's source text with minimal rearrangement, the theological point emerging more from the Chronicler's added refrain, 'the LORD made David victorious,' than from the placement itself.

debates.bearing: Either way, the effect for the reader is the same: God's covenant promise and God's historical action are shown to match, grounding the exiles' hope that the God who kept His word to David will keep His word to them.

debates.question: Is the priest in verse 16 Ahimelech son of Abiathar, as most Hebrew manuscripts read, or has father and son been reversed from 2 Samuel 8:17?

views.label: A scribal transposition
views.case: 2 Samuel 8:17 names Zadok and Ahimelech son of Abiathar in the reverse order, Abiathar son of Ahimelech, which matches what is known of the priestly line, Abiathar being the son of Ahimelech who died at Nob; some manuscripts and the Vulgate and Syriac here read Abimelech son of Abiathar, suggesting a very early transposition of names in transmission.

views.label: A recurring family name
views.case: Ahitub, Ahimelech, and Abiathar were recurring names across generations of this priestly family, so it is possible a grandson bore the name Ahimelech and served alongside Zadok in David's court, distinct from the Ahimelech who died at Nob.

debates.bearing: The identity of individual names does not affect the chapter's message; either reading confirms an established, functioning priesthood serving alongside David's just administration, part of the ordered worship the Chronicler prizes.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond yasha, qadash, and mas, several other words shape this chapter. The Philistines are first "subdued," kana, verse 1, the Hiphil of a root meaning to humble or bring low, the very verb Israel is later told to use of itself, "if My people... humble themselves," 2 Chronicles 7:14; the God who humbles Israel's enemies here is the same God who calls His own people to that same humbling, a telling symmetry the Chronicler's first readers, themselves recently humbled by exile, would have felt keenly.

The verb "struck down," nakah, recurs through nearly every campaign, verses 1, 2, 5, and 12, an ordinary word for military defeat that the Chronicler never varies or dresses up; its very plainness across four different enemies is part of the point, victory here is not a single dramatic miracle but a repeated, almost routine pattern, underlining that this is simply what happens when the LORD is with a king.

Twice David "places garrisons," netsib, verses 6 and 13, an administrative rather than merely military term, describing not a single battle won but an ongoing occupying presence that converts a defeated enemy into a stable, tribute paying subject, the very shape rest from every enemy takes in real ancient politics rather than the mere absence of fighting.

The officials named at the chapter's close carry meaningful titles of their own. Jehoshaphat is called the mazkir, verse 15, literally the one who causes to be remembered, a royal recorder whose office existed to keep the king's acts in memory, an office whose whole purpose quietly mirrors the Chronicler's own task centuries later, keeping Israel's history remembered rightly for a generation at risk of forgetting it. Shavsha is the sofer, scribe, verse 16, the trained writer who kept the court's official records, another office of memory and documentation standing at the very heart of David's government of justice.

Even Hadadezer's own name is telling. It combines Hadad, the Aramean storm god, with ezer, help, so that the king's name itself means something like "Hadad is my help," a claim the narrative quietly overturns; the god invoked in his own name proves powerless before the LORD who "made David victorious wherever he went."

Even the officers whose gold shields David carries off, verse 7, are called sarim, a general term for princes or commanders rather than common soldiers, marking these spoils as the personal, prestige gear of Hadadezer's own high command rather than ordinary battlefield salvage.

typology.type: The LORD who makes David victorious wherever he went
typology.fulfillment: David's campaigns won real but temporary ground, each defeated nation eventually needing to be subdued again by later kings, since the underlying power of hostile nations was never actually destroyed, only pushed back. Christ's triumph admits no such need for repetition. Where David hamstrung horses and left garrisons to enforce an uneasy peace, Christ, by dying and rising, disarmed the rulers and authorities outright, making a public spectacle of them, so that no garrison, treaty, or further campaign is required to keep what He has won, Colossians 2:15.

typology.type: Plunder dedicated to the LORD, later used to build the temple
typology.fulfillment: David could only offer what he had taken from others, metal stripped from defeated kings and carried home as spoil. Christ's giving reverses the direction entirely; He does not plunder others to build His house but empties Himself, giving His own life to purchase the very people who become the building material, living stones set upon Him as the cornerstone, 1 Peter 2:4-5. The gold that waited a generation in Jerusalem's storerooms before Solomon shaped it foreshadows a longer patience still, an already purchased people being built, over centuries, into a dwelling not yet finished.

typology.type: David's just and righteous administration for all his people
typology.fulfillment: David's justice depended on the competence and integrity of named officials, a recorder, priests, a scribe, a commander of the guard, any one of whom could fail or be replaced, and in fact several of these same offices later split their loyalty during Solomon's succession crisis, 1 Kings 1. The justice of David's greater Son depends on no such delegated, fallible machinery; He administers His kingdom in His own person, and Isaiah promises that of the increase of His government and of peace there will be no end, a permanence David's own capable cabinet could never guarantee.

study.christ:
The closing description of David's reign, that he "administered justice and righteousness for all his people," verse 14, is not filler before a list of names; it is the very phrase Jeremiah later uses to describe the coming Branch of David, "a King will reign wisely and administer justice and righteousness in the land," Jeremiah 23:5. The Chronicler's readers, holding both texts, would have heard David's own reign as a real but partial preview of a kingship still being awaited, the same words used of the son not yet arrived.

David's wars themselves anticipate a stranger sort of victory than his own. Zechariah pictures a king who comes not on warhorses and chariots like Hadadezer's captured thousand, but humble and riding on a donkey, and who commands peace to the nations rather than subduing them by force, Zechariah 9:9-10, a deliberate reversal of exactly the military machinery David dismantles in this chapter. Christ fulfills David's pattern of victory and Zechariah's pattern of peace at once, winning not by chariots but by the cross, and then commanding peace to those He has conquered rather than tribute.

Paul describes Christ's present reign in language that could serve as commentary on David's own campaign map, "He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet," 1 Corinthians 15:25, the ongoing subjugation David enacted province by province now unfolding as a single, cosmic reign moving toward its completion, when even death itself, the last enemy, is defeated.

And where this chapter shows a king whose victories, however God given, remain provisional, requiring garrisons and ongoing vigilance to hold, John pictures the final form of the same pattern: a rider called Faithful and True, waging war in righteousness, whose robe is already dipped in blood before the battle even begins, because the outcome was never actually in doubt, Revelation 19:11-16. David's victories were real installments on a debt that only this Rider finally and completely collects.
study.god:
God is shown here as the true giver of victory: twice the narrator interrupts the battle summary to insist that it is the LORD, not David, who wins these wars. God is also the God who receives what is rightly His, David's dedicated plunder becoming, in time, the material of God's own house. And God is the source of just government, since David's administration of justice and righteousness for his people flows from the character of the covenant God who rules over him. Even in war and empire building, the chapter's real subject is the faithfulness of God to His covenant word.

The chapter's God is also patient with the ordinary means through which He works. He does not remove Zobah's chariots directly; David's army still marches, still fights, still hamstrings horses and garrisons cities, real human action within which the LORD's decisive help operates, so that the text can credit the LORD entirely without denying that David's men did the actual fighting. This is the ordinary pattern of providence throughout Scripture, human agency fully engaged, divine sovereignty fully credited, neither cancelling the other.

God is also shown receiving worship that comes from unexpected quarters. Tou of Hamath, a foreign king with no covenant claim on Israel's God, nonetheless sends gifts and blessing when he hears what the LORD has done through David, verses 9 to 10, a small, early hint that the nations were always meant to be drawn toward, not merely conquered by, the God of Israel, Genesis 12:3.

And God is shown turning the spoils of violence toward worship rather than indulgence. The gold and bronze taken in war do not fund royal luxury; they are set apart, verse 11, and specifically earmarked, by the Chronicler's own later notice, for the temple that will bear God's name, so that even the ugliness of ancient warfare is folded, in this particular history, into the larger story of a God building Himself a dwelling among His people.

crossReferences.note: The tightly parallel account of these same campaigns; comparing the two shows the Chronicler reproducing the history almost exactly while adding his own emphatic refrain crediting the LORD, a small but deliberate editorial fingerprint on inherited material.

Israel's king was warned not to acquire great numbers of horses for himself; David's choice to hamstring all but a hundred of Hadadezer's captured chariot horses, verse 4, reads as quiet, voluntary obedience to that old restriction rather than the empire building it would have enabled.

Jeremiah promises a coming King from David's line who will reign wisely and administer justice and righteousness in the land, the identical phrase used of David's own reign in verse 14, so that David's government becomes the pattern language later applied to great David's greater Son.

Benaiah, commander of David's foreign guard here, verse 17, later leads the coronation procession that secures Solomon's throne against a rival claimant, showing the officials listed in this chapter still shaping Israel's history a generation on.

Records Solomon actually casting the bronze Sea, the pillars, and the temple's bronze articles, the very metal David dedicated a generation earlier from Tibhath and Cun, verse 8, so that this chapter's war spoils become, in time, literal temple furniture.

Tou of Hamath's unsolicited gifts and blessing on hearing of David's victories, verses 9-10, offer an early, small scale picture of the promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham's line.

This psalm's heading places its composition during exactly this war with Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah, and the striking down of Edom, letting readers hear David's private prayer of near despair, You have rejected us, underneath a chapter that otherwise reports only triumph.

Paul describes Christ's ongoing reign in language that could summarize David's whole campaign map, ruling until every enemy is put under His feet, the final, complete form of the subjugation David enacted piecemeal, nation by nation.

The rider called Faithful and True wages a final war in righteousness and treads the winepress of God's wrath, the consummated, unrepeatable version of what David's God given victories, however real, could only provisionally and temporarily achieve.

study.oneStory:
Genesis gave humanity a mandate to "have dominion" over creation, Genesis 1:28, a calling Adam surrendered to the serpent almost immediately. The book of Judges shows what life looks like under that lost dominion reversed, cycle after cycle of Israel oppressed by exactly the nations, Moab, Aram, and Philistia among them, that this chapter now shows subdued. What centuries of judges could only interrupt for a season, this one chapter records as settled, tribute paying subjection on every border, because the LORD, not a judge raised up in crisis, was fighting for His king.

The chapter's own refrain, that victory belongs to the LORD and not to David, keeps that older mandate from becoming a human achievement to boast in twice over. Israel is not simply recovering Adam's dominion by its own strength; it is receiving it again as gift, exactly as it was first given in the garden, undeserved and entirely of grace.

Yet even David's rest is not the final rest. His officials still had to keep the peace by force; his garrisons still had to be manned; his gold still waited, unused, for a temple not yet built. The chapter's dominion, real as it is, remains a working model rather than the finished thing.

Paul names the very last enemy still to be subdued, death itself, 1 Corinthians 15:26, an enemy David's armies could push back but never actually defeat. The prophets look further still, to a day when nations will beat swords into plowshares and study war no more, Isaiah 2:4, dominion finally exercised without violence at all. What David's victories anticipate in the shape of conquest, the new creation fulfills in the shape of peace, both flowing from the same throne, occupied at last by David's own greater Son.

quiz.q: What refrain does the Chronicler repeat twice to explain David's success in this chapter?

options.text: That the LORD made David victorious wherever he went, crediting God rather than David's own strength.
options.note: Verses 6 and 13 both state this refrain, the Chronicler's own theological commentary on the wars.

options.text: That David's armies were larger and better equipped than any surrounding nation.
options.note: The text never credits David's military size; it credits the LORD directly.

options.text: That David's officials administered the kingdom wisely.
options.note: True of verses 14-17, but the refrain about victory in verses 6 and 13 credits the LORD, not the officials.

options.text: That the surrounding nations were too weak to resist Israel.
options.note: Hadadezer's large armies, chariots, and allies show real, formidable opposition; victory is credited to the LORD, not to Israel's enemies being weak.

quiz.q: What did David do with the gold and silver he took from the defeated nations?

options.text: He dedicated it to the LORD, and some of the bronze was later used by Solomon to build the temple's Sea and pillars.
options.note: Verses 8 and 11 record David dedicating the plunder to the LORD rather than keeping it for himself.

options.text: He distributed it among his soldiers as a reward.
options.note: The text says nothing of a soldiers' reward here; the emphasis is on dedication to the LORD.

options.text: He kept it in his own treasury for personal use.
options.note: The opposite: David set the gold and silver apart for the LORD, not for himself.

options.text: He used it to build his own palace of cedar.
options.note: David did have a cedar palace, mentioned elsewhere, but this chapter specifically says the plunder was dedicated to the LORD, later feeding into the temple.

quiz.q: How does the chapter summarize David's reign over Israel?

options.text: He administered justice and righteousness for all his people, backed by a roster of officials, priests, and a scribe.
options.note: Verse 14 gives this summary, then verses 15-17 name the officials who carried it out.

options.text: He ruled mainly through military conquest and fear.
options.note: The chapter's summary is justice and righteousness, not fear or force.

options.text: He delegated all governing to Joab and the army.
options.note: Joab led the army, but the chapter names a fuller administration, recorder, priests, scribe, and royal sons, not military rule alone.

options.text: He reigned well, supported by a functioning government of named officials.
options.note: True, but this option omits the specific, pointed phrase 'justice and righteousness' that defines David's reign here.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Hamath's king sending gifts rather than fighting David?

options.text: It shows nations at a distance recognizing and submitting to David's God given dominion without even being conquered directly.
options.note: Tou of Hamath sends his son with gifts to bless David for defeating his rival Hadadezer, verses 9-10, extending David's influence beyond the battlefield.

options.text: It shows Hamath conquering David and demanding tribute.
options.note: The reverse: Hamath's king sends gifts of homage to David, not the other way around.

options.text: It shows an alliance of equals with no acknowledgment of David's superior standing.
options.note: The gifts and the language of blessing indicate Hamath honoring David's greater position, not a treaty of equals.

options.text: It shows David demanding tribute from Hamath by force.
options.note: Close, but the text specifically presents Tou acting voluntarily, sending gifts in gratitude and homage rather than under direct military compulsion.

quiz.q: How does David's pattern of victory point forward to Christ?

options.text: As the LORD gave David real but partial victories, Christ, the Son of David, has won total and final victory over every hostile power.
options.note: Colossians 2:15 describes Christ's complete triumph, of which David's wars are a partial, historical foreshadowing.

options.text: It shows that Christ's kingdom will also depend on human armies and conquest.
options.note: The New Testament describes Christ's victory as spiritual and complete, not achieved through human armies.

options.text: It shows only that David was a skilled general worth imitating in leadership.
options.note: The chapter's own emphasis undercuts this, crediting the LORD rather than David's skill.

options.text: It shows a pattern of God given success that later kings could also expect automatically.
options.note: Partly true, but the promise was specifically tied to God's covenant with David's house, not a generic guarantee to every later king.

questions: Twice the text insists 'the LORD made David victorious.' Where in your own life are you tempted to credit your strength, planning, or skill for something that was really God's gift?
David dedicated the plunder of his wars to the LORD rather than keeping it for himself. What would it look like for you to dedicate the fruit of your work, time, or success back to God this week?
The chapter closes by naming David's officials, not just his victories. Why do you think ordered, faithful administration matters as much to God as dramatic battlefield wins?
Distant Hamath sent gifts simply on hearing of David's victories. How does knowing that Christ's victory is already total change the way you face opposition or fear today?
David's justice and righteousness for all his people anticipates the perfect reign of Christ. Where do you long to see that justice and righteousness break into your own community or nation?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote gives an alternate rendering, 'the LORD saved David,' for 'the LORD made David victorious,' both translating the same Hebrew root, yasha, to save or deliver.

Some Hebrew manuscripts, along with the Vulgate and Syriac, read 'Ahimelech son of Abiathar,' matching this verse; most Hebrew manuscripts read 'Abimelech,' and the parallel in 2 Samuel 8:17 reverses the names to 'Abiathar son of Ahimelech.' The identity does not affect the chapter's meaning.

Shavsha the scribe is also called Seraiah, Sheva, and Shisha in other passages, 2 Samuel 8:17, 2 Samuel 20:25, and 1 Kings 4:3, likely reflecting spelling variation across sources rather than different people.
